account: Malawi's June 2017 measles vaccination campaign (Measles & Rubella Initiative) targeted more than 7.5 million children. The American Red Cross's Missing Maps team needed base maps for campaign monitoring. Facebook's population maps come from a machine-learning computer-vision method that detects buildings in satellite imagery. They were used to identify where people lived and which areas were already mapped in OpenStreetMap. Concentrating volunteers on settlements filtered out 97.1% of the land area. That reduced the area to map from 94,080 km² to 2,745 km² and completed the base map in a fraction of the normal time. The base map was to feed a dashboard for government and Red Cross monitors during the campaign. The article predates the campaign and reports no monitoring outcome. No vaccination-coverage outcome attributable to the maps is reported.

ai_role.statement: The Facebook settlement data determined where volunteer mapping effort went and which areas were skipped. The campaign itself was a Measles & Rubella Initiative effort supported by the American Red Cross and other partners, with monitors from the national government. The Red Cross attributes efficiency, not coverage, to the maps. The Red Cross account is the implementing organization's and names only “Facebook's population datasets”, without mentioning machine learning. The identification with the High Resolution Settlement Layer and the machine-learning description are taken from the vendor-authored Tiecke et al. preprint. It does not mention the Malawi campaign.

claim_basis: Sources: the makers' preprint and two press releases from the deployer. The cited evidence includes no independent source and no finding by a regulator or court.

comparator.against: mapping the whole national land area without the settlement maps (the normal Missing Maps approach)
comparator.quote: Much of Malawi is rural, so concentrating on population settlements allowed us to filter out 97.1% of the total land area that we sought to map. This technique reduced our mapping area from 94,080km2 to 2,745 km2. Volunteers could then spend their time mapping communities instead of searching through acres of uninhabited areas; they were able to complete the mapping in a fraction of the normal time.

later.note: After the June 2017 campaign the Red Cross's Missing Maps team reported that the traced base map underpinned a real-time monitoring dashboard covering 13,743 children, and again credited Facebook's population data with filtering uninhabited areas out of the tracing tasks.
later.quote: We are also grateful for Facebook’s high-resolution population data for Malawi, which helped us to identify areas with and without concentrations of people. This made the tracing much, much faster – we filtered uninhabited areas out of the tracing tasks so that we could direct remote mappers towards areas that had features for them to map.

fields.account: Malawi's June 2017 measles vaccination campaign (Measles & Rubella Initiative) targeted more than 7.5 million children. The American Red Cross's Missing Maps team needed base maps for campaign monitoring. Facebook's population maps come from a machine-learning computer-vision method that detects buildings in satellite imagery. They were used to identify where people lived and which areas were already mapped in OpenStreetMap. Concentrating volunteers on settlements filtered out 97.1% of the land area. That reduced the area to map from 94,080 km² to 2,745 km² and completed the base map in a fraction of the normal time. The base map was to feed a dashboard for government and Red Cross monitors during the campaign. The article predates the campaign and reports no monitoring outcome. No vaccination-coverage outcome attributable to the maps is reported.
